'''Jerzy Maria Weyman''' (Polish pronunciation: [ˈjɛʐɨ ˈveyman]; born April 29, 1955)<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://jerzyweyman.com/bio/|title=Bio|website=Jerzy Weyman}}</ref> is a [[Polish-American]] [[mathematician]] whose field is [[algebra]]. With over four decades of professional expertise, he has authored more than 100 publications in peer-reviewed journals and has written two books.

==Biography==
Weyman was born on April 29, 1955, in [[Toruń]], [[Poland]], into a family with a rich history, including notable figures from [[Poland|Polish]] history and literature. His maternal great-great-grandfather, Count [[Aleksander Fredro]], was a poet and playwright from the era of [[Polish Romanticism]], while his great-grandfather, [[Piotr Szembek]], served as a military general in the 19th century.<ref>[https://www.sejm-wielki.pl/b/zi.7.103.a8a2 M.J. Minakowski, Genealogy of the Descendants of The Great Parliament]</ref> Weyman's father's family immigrated to [[Poland]] from [[Alsace]] in the 19th century, where the surname Weyman is common.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://ancestors.familysearch.org/en/K895-B5B/johann-weymann-1829-1907|title=FamilySearch.org|website=ancestors.familysearch.org}}</ref> Both of Weyman's parents were doctors.

His interest in [[mathematics]] began in the 4th grade at IV LO [High School in [[Toruń]], where a teacher inspired him. Enrolling in the [[Faculty of Mathematics]] at [[Nicolaus Copernicus University]] of Toruń in 1973, Weyman developed a passion for [[algebra]], particularly influenced by his mentor Tadeusz Józefiak. The same year, Weyman won a bronze medal at the [[International Mathematical Olympiad]] in Moscow.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.deltami.edu.pl/media/articles/1974/01/delta-1974-01-nasi-na-olimpiadzie.pdf|title=Poles at the Olympics}}</ref>

In 1977, Weyman defended his master's thesis on ideals generated by monomials. He became an [[assistant professor]] at the [[Mathematical Institute]] of the [[Polish Academy of Sciences]]. He later pursued graduate studies at [[Brandeis University]] in the [[US]], completing his [[Ph.D.]] in 1980 on free resolutions of determinantal ideals. Weyman returned to [[Poland]] in the early 1980s, continuing his role at the Mathematical Institute and collaborating on [[commutative algebra]] problems. In 1982, he received the Award of the [[Polish Mathematical Society]] for Young Mathematicians, and in 1984, he became a laureate of the [[Kazimierz Kuratowski Prize]] along with Piotr Pragacz.<ref name="auto1">{{Cite web|url=https://www.impan.pl/en/events/awards/kazimierz-kuratowski|title=Kazimierz Kuratowski Award}}</ref>

In 1985, Weyman permanently moved to the [[United States]], becoming an [[assistant professor]] at [[Northeastern University]] of [[Boston]]. He rose to the rank of [[full professor]] in 1995. His academic journey involved collaborations with renowned mathematicians, such as [[David Buchsbaum]], [[David Eisenbud]], [[Harm Derksen]], [[Kiyoshi Igusa]], [[Marc Levine (mathematician)|Marc Levine]], [[Joseph Landsberg]], [[Gordana Todorov]] and [[Andrei Zelevinsky]]. In 2003, he published his first book, "Cohomology of Vector Bundles and Syzygies." He received the [[Humboldt Research Award]] in 2012.<ref name="auto">{{Cite web|url=https://www.humboldt-foundation.de/vernetzen/recherche-im-humboldt-netzwerk/einzelansicht?tx_rsmavhsolr_solrviewhumboldtians%5BpPersonId%5D=1145736&cHash=05509d95c037d5675aa68527e1e24a58|title=Prof. Dr. Jerzy Weyman|website=www.humboldt-foundation.de}}</ref>

In 2013, Weyman joined the [[University of Connecticut]] as the Stuart and Joan Sidney [[Professor of Mathematics]].<ref name="auto5">{{Cite web|url=https://simons.berkeley.edu/people/jerzy-weyman|title=Jerzy Weyman|website=Simons Institute for the Theory of Computing}}</ref> He contributed to the [[Commutative Algebra]] Special Year at [[Simons Laufer Mathematical Sciences Institute|MSRI]] and received the title of [[professor]] in [[Poland]].<ref>Decree of the president of the Republic of Poland dated June 3, 2013, No. 115-6-13 regarding the conferment of the title of professor. ({{Monitor Polski|2013|593}}).</ref> In 2015, he was awarded the [[Wacław Sierpiński]] Medal and Lecture.<ref name="auto4">{{cite web |access-date=2023-09-02 |title=Sierpiński Medal {{!}} MIMUW |url=https://www.mimuw.edu.pl/en/sierpinski-medal |website=www.mimuw.edu.pl}}<!-- auto-translated from Polish by Module:CS1 translator --></ref><ref name="auto2">{{cite web |access-date=2023-09-02 |title=Wacław Sierpiński Medal and Lecture {{!}} Polish Mathematical Society |url=https://www.ptm.org.pl/konkursy/wyklady-im-waclawa-sierpinskiego |website=www.ptm.org.pl}}<!-- auto-translated from Polish by Module:CS1 translator --></ref> In 2017, Weyman co-authored the book "Introduction to Quiver Representations." After 34 years in the U.S., he returned to [[Poland]] in 2019, joining [[Jagiellonian University]]. In 2021, he received the [[Stefan Banach Prize]] from the [[Polish Mathematical Society]] for outstanding achievements in [[mathematical sciences]].<ref name="auto3">{{Cite web|url=https://im.uj.edu.pl/ogloszenia/aktualnosci/-/journal_content/56_INSTANCE_L2yp/65632/147613421|title=Aktualności - Instytut Matematyki Uniwersytetu Jagiellońskiego|website=im.uj.edu.pl}}</ref> Weyman continues his work at [[Jagiellonian University]], leading various research projects, most notably implementing a research grant focused on Applications of Lie algebras to Commutative Algebra, such as Research in commutative algebra and representation theory<ref>[https://projekty.ncn.gov.pl/index.php?projekt_id=452409 Research in commutative algebra and representation theory]</ref> and Structure of equivariant D-modules.<ref>[https://projekty.ncn.gov.pl/index.php?projekt_id=408619 Structure of equivariant D-modules]</ref>
